name: Candombe — Madera (Clave)
desc: The Afro-Uruguayan candombe timeline struck on the wooden drum shell, dividing the 16-pulse cycle irregularly as 3+3+4+2+4 with only two strokes landing on the beat. It governs the entire cuerda of three drums.
source: Jure & Rocamora, 'Clave patterns in Uruguayan Candombe drumming' (candombeando.uy / iie.fing.edu.uy/~rocamora/phdthesis/candombe.html)

name: Candombe — Chico (steady high drum)
desc: The chico defines the tatum, a rapid continuous pulse, but tellingly does not articulate the pulse falling on the beat — its strongest accent lands on the second tatum of each beat, giving candombe its forward lean.
source: Rocamora PhD thesis, Universidad de la República (iie.fing.edu.uy/~rocamora/phdthesis/candombe.html)

name: Candombe — Piano (low drum)
desc: The piano drum plays the lowest, most syncopated voice; its pattern is congruent with the madera clave, reinforcing the four-beat cycle with heavy downbeat emphasis.
source: Rocamora PhD thesis (iie.fing.edu.uy/~rocamora/phdthesis/candombe.html); Jure & Rocamora 2017

name: Candombe — Repique (improvising drum)
desc: The medium-pitched repique has the greatest freedom of the cuerda, weaving syncopated variations and the madera between phrases to generate surprise and variety over the chico and piano.
source: Rocamora PhD thesis (iie.fing.edu.uy/~rocamora/phdthesis/candombe.html)

name: Candombe Porteño (Buenos Aires)
desc: The Afro-Argentine candombe of Buenos Aires, played on llamador (bass) and repicador (sharp) drums; through the milonga it is a recognized root of tango.
source: Wikipedia 'Candombe'; turismo.buenosaires.gob.ar 'Discover the rhythm of the city's roots'

name: Marinera Norteña
desc: Peru's national coastal courtship dance from the north, built on the 6/8–3/4 sesquiáltera: guitar and cajón outline the compound-duple 6/8 against a triple-meter 3/4 bass pulse.
source: Wikipedia 'Marinera'; Smithsonian Folklife Festival 'Marinera Dance'

name: Marinera Limeña (de salón)
desc: The refined Lima salon marinera, slower and more elegant than the northern form, keeping the same 6/8 lilt with sesquiáltera between the guitar's 6/8 and a 3/4 cajón pulse.
source: Wikipedia 'Marinera'; mundoandino.com 'Marinera'

name: Tondero
desc: A fast northern-Peruvian coastal dance close kin to the marinera; its accelerating cajón 'golpe de tierra' repique drives a 6/8-against-3/4 sesquiáltera.
source: Wikipedia 'Tondero'; illapa.com 'Typical Dances of the Peruvian Coast'

name: Festejo
desc: The festive Afro-Peruvian dance whose cajón 'golpe' drives a 6/8 accent pattern over a 3/4 frame, with cajita and quijada answering; percussion is the rhythmic core.
source: Wikipedia 'Festejo'; Cal Performances program notes 'Perú Negro'

name: Landó
desc: A slow, sensual Afro-Peruvian form whose ambiguous subdivision is most accurately felt in 12/8; the cajón weaves between 6/4 and 3/4 readings, the deepest sesquiáltera of the coast.
source: Toussaint et al., 'The Geometry of the Peruvian Landó' (ResearchGate); Morales, 'Afro-Peruvian Percussion Ensemble' (Sher Music)

name: Zamacueca
desc: The 19th-century Afro-Peruvian ancestor of marinera and Chilean cueca, notated in 12/8 or 6/4, with cajón outlining the 6/8-versus-3/4 hemiola at the heart of the cueca family.
source: pancocojams.blogspot.com 'Zamacueca & Festejo'; Morales, 'Afro-Peruvian Percussion Ensemble' (Sher Music)

name: Vals Criollo (Peruvian Waltz)
desc: The Peruvian creole waltz in 3/4 with the guitar's 'tundete' bordón-on-1 pattern and Afro-Peruvian cajón syncopation; subtle hemiola (3/4 against 6/8) gives it sway.
source: 'Patrones rítmicos del vals criollo peruano' (ResearchGate); fertur-travel.com 'Vals Peruano'

name: Huayno (Peruvian)
desc: The quintessential Andean highland dance in brisk duple meter with a strong downbeat, bright pentatonic melodies and the characteristic short-long huayno galloping cell.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Peru'; melodigging.com 'Huayno'

name: Yaraví (Harawi)
desc: A slow, plaintive Andean song of pre-Hispanic harawi origin, freely metered across 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4; here a languid triple-time lament that often precedes a huayno.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Peru'; melodigging.com 'Huayno' (harawi)

name: Cueca Chilena
desc: Chile's national courtship dance, the textbook sesquiáltera: guitar and palmas strum a 6/8 while the bombo and harp bass mark a 3/4, the two meters in constant tension.
source: Wikipedia 'Cueca'; Berklee PULSE 'Basic Cueca Guitar Strumming Pattern'; marcachile.cl 'Types of Cueca'

name: Cueca Nortina
desc: The instrumental, wordless cueca of northern Chile driven by brass bands, bombo and trumpet, keeping the 6/8-versus-3/4 hemiola of the southern sung cueca.
source: Wikipedia 'Cueca'; marcachile.cl 'La cueca, espejo de nuestra diversidad cultural'

name: Tonada Chilena
desc: A lyrical strophic song of central Chile at moderate-to-slow tempo, carried by guitar and arpa chilena, alternating Iberian sesquiáltera with a plain 3/4.
source: melodigging.com 'Tonada Chilena'; musicadechile.org 'La Tonada'

name: Chacarera
desc: The energetic dance of Santiago del Estero: the bombo legüero pounds rim-and-head accents in 6/8 while the guitar syncopates and the bass implies 3/4, a textbook hemiola at ~130 bpm.
source: Wikipedia/Argentine folklore sources; tango-dj.at 'Chacarera'; UNLP 'Bombo legüero' thesis (sedici.unlp.edu.ar)

name: Chacarera Doble
desc: The longer, more driving variant of the chacarera with extended phrases; the bombo legüero intensifies the 6/8-over-3/4 sesquiáltera of the standard form.
source: tango-dj.at 'Chacarera'; UNLP 'Bombo legüero' methodological thesis (sedici.unlp.edu.ar)

name: Zamba (Argentine)
desc: A slow, graceful handkerchief dance descended from the zamacueca; flowing 6/8 guitar arpeggios over soft bombo, keeping a gentler 6/8-versus-3/4 lilt than the chacarera.
source: Argentine folklore sources (argentina-excepcion.com; wander-argentina.com 'Argentine Folk Music')

name: Gato
desc: A lively, witty Argentine couple dance sharing the chacarera's binary-versus-ternary game; rapid 6/8 guitar and bombo against an implied 3/4 bass.
source: tangoallegria.it 'Argentine Dances'; melodigging.com 'Folklore Argentino'

name: Escondido
desc: A playful 'hide-and-seek' dance kin to the gato, sharing the chacarera's 6/8-over-3/4 sesquiáltera with characteristic bombo accents and choreographic pauses.
source: scribd 'Argentine Folk Rhythms Workshop Guide'; tangoallegria.it 'Argentine Dances'

name: Malambo
desc: The intense solo gaucho zapateo: relentless percussive footwork answered by a driving bombo legüero in 6/8, the dancer's heels cutting across the 3/4 accent grid.
source: Argentine folklore sources (argentine-tango.net 'chacarera, zamba, malambo'); fr.wikipedia 'Bombo (instrument)'

name: Milonga Campera
desc: The slow rural milonga of the Buenos Aires pampas, sung by payadores over a single guitar's bordoneo with the 3-3-2 habanera-derived bass cell.
source: Wikipedia 'Milonga (music)'; pianospuch.com.ar 'Milonga Campera'

name: Milonga Ciudadana (Porteña)
desc: The faster urban milonga of tango orchestras, built on the habanera cell (dotted-eighth, sixteenth, two eighths) that gives milonga porteña its definitive bounce.
source: tangotopics.com 'Habanera Rhythm'; adamtully.com 'Rhythms or Genres in tango'

name: Tango — Habanera (Guardia Vieja)
desc: Early 'dos por cuatro' tango of the old guard, danced over the habanera bass cell inherited from the milonga, naturally notated in 2/4.
source: symposium.music.org 'Music Theory and the Tango'; tangology101.com 'Structure of Argentine Tango'

name: Tango — Marcato (4/4)
desc: The driving 'marcato in 4' of the dance orchestras (Di Sarli, D'Arienzo): an accented quarter-note pulse on every beat that dancers walk to in the basic step.
source: adamtully.com 'Rhythms or Genres in tango'; tangology101.com 'Structure of Argentine Tango Part 2'

name: Tango — Yumba (Pugliese)
desc: Osvaldo Pugliese's dramatic 'yumba' accent: a heavy syncopated push-pull where bass and piano stab just ahead of beats 1 and 3, then release, giving the orchestra its lurching intensity.
source: adamtully.com 'Rhythms or Genres in tango'; Emory Music 'Faces of Tango'

name: Vals Criollo Argentino (Tango Waltz)
desc: The Argentine tango-waltz (vals criollo) in lilting 3/4, with the bass on the strong first beat and a gentle one-two-three sway under flowing melodic lines.
source: adamtully.com 'Rhythms or Genres in tango'; Wikipedia 'Vals criollo'

name: Carnavalito
desc: The festive Andean round-dance of northwest Argentina and Bolivia in bright duple meter, driven by caja, bombo, charango and quena with a relentless huayno-like pulse.
source: Argentine/Andean folklore sources (melodigging.com 'Folklore Argentino'); Wikipedia 'Carnavalito'

name: Caporales
desc: The athletic Bolivian carnival dance born from the Afro-Andean saya of the Yungas; brass bands and bombo drive a syncopated duple groove with the famous off-beat caporales kick.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; bolivianthoughts.com 'Bolivian folklore 101: Caporales'

name: Saya (Afro-Bolivian)
desc: The percussive Afro-Bolivian saya of the Yungas, whose interlocking bombos sound a 'double palpitation' over call-and-response song; the rhythmic root of caporales.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; guidebolivia.com 'Traditional dances of Bolivia'

name: Tinku
desc: The combative ritual dance-music of northern Potosí: a loud, constant warlike bombo beat in duple meter under charangos and zampoñas, mirroring the stomping 'encounter'.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; guidebolivia.com 'Traditional dances of Bolivia'

name: Morenada
desc: The stately, heavy-stepping Afro-Andean dance of Oruro carnival; brass and the deep wankara/bombo dictate a slow, dragging duple march evoking enslaved Africans' chained gait.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; remote-expeditions.com 'Music a Dances in Bolivia'

name: Diablada
desc: The masked 'dance of the devils' that is the emblem of Oruro carnival; brass bands and bombo march a vigorous duple meter staging the battle of good against evil.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; guidebolivia.com 'Traditional dances of Bolivia'

name: Tobas
desc: An energetic Bolivian dance depicting eastern-lowland jungle tribes, with abrupt leaping steps over a fast, pounding duple bombo drive.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; guidebolivia.com 'Traditional dances of Bolivia'

name: Huayño (Bolivian)
desc: The Bolivian highland huayño, a popular 2/4 Altiplano dance with a strong downbeat and the short-long galloping cell, underpinning charango and zampoña melodies.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Bolivia'; melodigging.com 'Bolivian Huayño'

name: Sanjuanito
desc: Ecuador's emblematic indigenous highland dance in lively 2/4, festive and processional, with bombo and rondador over a strong duple downbeat.
source: ecuadorianmusic.wordpress.com 'Highlands'; UTN repository 'Pasacalle, Sanjuanito y Bomba'

name: Bomba del Chota
desc: The Afro-Ecuadorian dance of the Chota Valley, its bomba drum laying a 6/8 accent against a 3/4 pulse — a sesquiáltera shared with the Andean-Afro coast.
source: Wikipedia 'Bomba (Ecuador)'; allaroundthisworld.com 'Ecuador: Bomba del Chota'

name: Albazo
desc: A lively Ecuadorian highland genre traditionally played at dawn, built on a 6/8 guitar and bombo pattern crossing a 3/4 bass in characteristic sesquiáltera.
source: ecuadorianmusic.wordpress.com 'Highlands'; UAzuay '07183' (pasillo, albazo)

name: Pasillo Ecuatoriano
desc: Ecuador's melancholic national song genre in slow 3/4, descended from the European waltz, with arpeggiated guitar and gentle hemiolic sway under sentimental melodies.
source: walnutcreekband.org 'Folk Music From Ecuador'; UAzuay '07183' (pasillo, albazo)

name: Polka Paraguaya (Polca)
desc: Paraguay's signature dance: a strong sesquiáltera where the bass marks a simple triple 3/4 while harp and guitar melodies group the bar as compound-duple 6/8.
source: Wikipedia 'Paraguayan polka'; Smithsonian Folkways 'Colorful Genres in Harp music from Paraguay'

name: Galopa Paraguaya
desc: A faster, more festive variant of the polka paraguaya played by galoperas; the binary-ternary overlap intensifies into a driving 6/8-against-3/4 gallop.
source: Wikipedia 'Paraguayan polka'; musicaparaguaya.jimdofree.com 'Types of folk music'

name: Guarania
desc: José Asunción Flores's slow, melancholic Paraguayan genre, drawing the polka's binary-ternary overlap down to a brooding 6/8 with a gentle 3/4 undertow.
source: Wikipedia 'Music of Paraguay'; musicaparaguaya.jimdofree.com 'Types of folk music'

name: Pasillo Lento (Colombo-Andean)
desc: The slow salon pasillo of the northern Andes in 3/4, with a tres-against-dos hemiola felt against the guitar bordón, kin to the Ecuadorian and Venezuelan forms.
source: walnutcreekband.org 'Folk Music From Ecuador'; ecuadorianmusic.wordpress.com 'Highlands'

name: Cueca Brava (Urbana)
desc: The urban 'cueca brava' of Santiago's working-class quarters, sung by cuequeros over piano, guitar and panderos, keeping the 6/8-versus-3/4 sesquiáltera at brisk tempo.
source: marcachile.cl 'Types of Cueca'; Wikipedia 'Cueca'

name: Vidala
desc: A solemn pre-Hispanic-rooted song of northwest Argentina, sung in thirds over the steady pulse of the caja vidalera; a slow ternary lament inside the 6/8–3/4 frame.
source: melodigging.com 'Folklore Argentino'; UNLP 'Bombo legüero' thesis (sedici.unlp.edu.ar)
